title: File information
lead: Use file, stat, ls -l, ln -s, readlink and realpath to read a file's real type, size, times and link target.
objectives: You know that on Linux an extension is just a name and `file` shows the real type.
You read size, permissions, owner and times with `stat` and `ls -l`.
You create symbolic links and find their target with `ls -l`, `readlink` and `realpath`.

sections.title: Real type: file
body: On Windows you tell the type from the extension. On Linux `.jpg` is only a name; the content can be something else entirely. `file` ignores the extension and looks at the first bytes of the content.
This helps with downloaded files: a file called `image.jpg` may really be an executable program.

commands.what: Tells the real file type from its content.
commands.why: Exposes wrong extensions and disguised files.

commands.what: Prints the type as a MIME type (e.g. text/plain).
commands.where: In scripts and web server configuration.

sections.tip: In the output, `ASCII text` means text, `ELF` an executable program and `directory` a folder.

sections.title: Details: stat and ls -l
body: `ls -l` shows type, permissions, owner, size and date on one line. `stat` gives more: inode, link count and three timestamps.

Times: **Access** last read, **Modify** last change of the content, **Change** last change of metadata such as permissions or owner. The first character shows the type: `-` file, `d` folder, `l` symbolic link.

commands.what: Shows all technical details of a file.
commands.where: When you need exact size, permissions and times.
For a quick look into a folder.
commands.why: Type, permissions, owner, size and date on one line.
A readable size instead of a byte count.

commands.what: Lists the folder itself, not its contents.

sections.tip: `ls -lh` rounds; for exact bytes use `stat` or `wc -c`.

sections.title: Symbolic links and the real path
body: A symbolic link (symlink) is a small file that points to another path. `ls -l` shows it as `link.txt -> data.txt`. If the target is missing the link is **broken**: it exists, but opening it gives an error.
Deleting a link does not delete the target; `rm link.txt` removes only the link. `readlink` prints the target one step, `realpath` the fully resolved absolute path.

commands.what: Creates a symbolic link: target first, then link name.
commands.why: Access under a second name without copying.

commands.what: Prints the target a link points to.
commands.where: When you want to know where a link goes.
commands.why: In scripts you get the target cleanly.

commands.what: Prints the absolute path with all links resolved.
commands.where: With relative paths or chains of links.
commands.why: Shows the file's real location on disk.

sections.warn: The target path is relative to the link's folder. `ln -s data.txt ~/info/link.txt` works; `ln -s data.txt ~/link.txt` from another folder creates a broken link.

sections.title: Name and size: basename, dirname, wc
body: `basename` returns the last part of a path, `dirname` the folder part. Both are common in scripts for splitting paths.
`wc -c` gives the size in bytes, `wc -l` the number of lines.

commands.what: Prints the last component (file name) of a path.
commands.where: In scripts when you only need the name.
commands.why: No need to cut the path by hand.

commands.what: Prints the folder part of a path.
commands.where: To find the folder of a file.
commands.why: You get the folder without the file name.

commands.what: Prints the byte count of a file.
commands.where: When you need the exact size.

t01.text: Run `stat` on `~/info/data.txt` and find the Size and Modify lines.

t02.text: List the folder `~/info` in long format.

t03.text: Print only the file name of the path `~/info/data.txt` with `basename`.

t04.text: Print the folder part of the same path with `dirname`.

t05.text: List the contents of `~/info` with readable sizes.

t06.text: How many bytes is `data.txt`? Find out with `wc -c`.
t06.hint: Three lines: alpha, beta, gamma; each has a line ending.

t07.text: Find the number of lines of `data.txt` with `wc -l`.

t08.text: Create the symbolic link `~/info/link.txt` with the target `data.txt`.
t08.hint: `ln -s data.txt ~/info/link.txt`; the target is relative to the link's folder.

t09.text: Predict: how does the link look in the output of `ls -l ~/info`? Run it and check.
t09.hint: You see `link.txt -> data.txt` and an `l` at the start.

t11.text: Predict: which letter does the line of `ls -ld ~/info` start with? Run it.

t12.text: Predict: what does `stat` do for the non-existent `~/info/missing.txt`? Run it.
t12.hint: It fails: No such file or directory.

t13.text: Try a broken link: create a link without target using `ln -s nothing.txt ~/broken`, then run `cat ~/broken`.
t13.hint: The link exists, the target does not; `cat` reports an error.

t14.text: Debug: `~/info/picture.jpg` is really plain text. Rename it to `picture.txt`.
t14.hint: Look inside with `cat`, then rename with `mv`.

t15.text: Mini project: create the folder `~/inventory`, write a file with `echo version1 > ~/inventory/v1.txt`, create the link `current` with target `v1.txt` and verify with `ls -l ~/inventory`.

t16.text: Hard task: create `~/shortcut` as a link to `~/info/data.txt`, inspect it with `ls -l ~/shortcut` and `stat ~/shortcut`, then delete the link. `data.txt` must remain.
t16.hint: `rm` removes only the link and does not touch the target.

t17.text: Ticket #2520: The audit team wants the size of `~/info/data.txt` in bytes in the file `~/size.txt`. Redirect the output into the file.

vm.intro: Try it on your VM. There are no destructive commands here; you only create small test files in your home directory.

v01.title: Find the real type
v01.text: Run `file` on a text file, a program and a folder and paste the output.

blocks.expected:
/etc/hostname: ASCII text
/usr/bin/ls:  ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, ...
/etc:         directory

differs: The location of `ls` depends on the distribution; find it with `which ls`.
If `file` is missing, install it with `sudo apt install file` on Ubuntu or `sudo dnf install file` on Rocky/Alma.

v02.title: The lying extension
v02.text: Give a text file the name `.jpg` and see what `file` says.
differs: Your path may be `/home/alice/fake.jpg`; the word `text` is what matters.

v03.title: Details with stat
v03.text: Find the Size, Modify and Change lines in the `stat` output.

blocks.expected:
File: /home/student/fake.jpg
  Size: 6   Blocks: 8   regular file
Access: (0644/-rw-r--r--) ...
Modify: 2026-01-01 10:00:00 ...

differs: On a localised system labels may be translated; `LANG=C stat ~/fake.jpg` prints English.
The Birth line is `-` on some file systems.

v04.title: Link and real path
v04.text: Create a symbolic link and find the target with `ls -l`, `readlink` and `realpath`.
differs: If `->` is missing in the `ls -l` output, check the order of `ln -s` (target first, then link name).
If `realpath` is missing, `readlink -f ~/pic_link` does the same.

v05.title: Clean up
v05.text: Delete the test files. If there were no errors, press "Done".
differs: `rm` removes the link first, then the target file. In reverse order the link stays broken, which is harmless.

q1.q: What does `file image.jpg` use to determine a file's type?
options: The first bytes of its content
q1.explain: On Linux the extension is only a name; `file` checks the content.

q2.q: What does the Modify time in `stat` output show?
q2.explain: Modify is the content time, Change the metadata time, Access the last read.

q3.q: What happens when you run `rm link.txt` on a symbolic link?
q3.explain: A link is its own entry; deleting it does not touch the target.

q4.q: Which command prints the absolute path with all links resolved?
q4.explain: `realpath` resolves relative paths and link chains into the real absolute path.

summary: An extension is only a name; use `file` for the real type.
`ls -l` is the quick overview, `stat` the details; Modify is content time, Change metadata time.
`ln -s target link` creates a symbolic link; `ls -l` shows `->`.
`readlink` shows the target, `realpath` the full absolute path; `rm link` does not delete the target.

glossary.meaning: A special file that points to another path.
The metadata record of a file in the file system.
A symbolic link whose target does not exist.
A label for the content type, e.g. text/plain.
